title: Assistive listening devices for improving auditory processing and school performance of children with special needs (dyslexia, hyperacusis/misophonia, autism spectrum disorder, learning/intellectual/multiple disabilities which include learning/intellectual disabilities)
summary:
Children can have problems processing and understanding what they hear in the brain, even though their ears function normally. Such disorders are called auditory processing disorders (APD). They can be treated with speech therapy or remote microphone hearing systems (RMHS), among other methods. Although the definition of APD excludes mental impairments, disorders with such impairments, including autism spectrum disorders (ASD), also appear to be associated with significant auditory processing difficulties. Currently, in germany, children receive a RMHS only if they have a specific form of APD, namely, if they have poor comprehension of speech in noisy environments and if intellectual impairment is excluded. However, research suggests that children with other auditory processing problems, e.g., reading and spelling disorders, noise hypersensitivity, ASD or learning/mental disabilities, could also benefit from such a facility. Attention, learning, classroom behaviour and cooperation, school success, self-esteem, and personal development can all be enhanced through the use of such devices. Even short-term use might lead to long-term improvements in the brain's processing of auditory signals. We, the study team, expect that even small improvements in understanding teachers in a noisy classroom through a RMHS could be critical to these children's success in school. 
Thus, the study aims to answer the following questions: do children with special problems or conditions such as reading and spelling disorders, hypersensitivity to certain sounds, autism, learning disabilities, intellectual disabilities, or multiple disabilities benefit from a wireless signal transmission system?  Do their auditory processing and perception skills, communication, behaviour, and school performance improve with it compared to before or, for reading and right-writing disorders only, to children receiving learning therapy only?
For this purpose, 93 school children aged 6 to 18 years with auditory processing difficulties with the above-mentioned diseases are assigned to five groups:
- Group I: 24 children with a reading and spelling disorder will receive standard learning therapy. This is provided by a learning therapist, such as a psychologist or teacher. They also receive a RMHS for 12 weeks.
- Group II: 24 children with a reading and spelling disorder undergo learning therapy only.
- Group III: 15 children with hypersensitivity to loud sounds or sounds perceived as unpleasant will receive a RMHS for 12 weeks.
- Group IV: 15 children with autism receive a RMHS for 12 weeks. 
- Group V: 15 children with a learning disability, intellectual disability, or multiple disabilities with intelligence reduction will receive a RMHS for 12 weeks.
Group assignment between Group I and II will be randomly selected. Only Roger Focus brand devices from Phonak will be used to keep conditions the same for all children and to make the study results comparable; the devices will be loaned by a hearing care professional. 
All children will be assessed at study entry, after the 12 weeks of treatment, and 6 months after completion of the 12-week treatment with comprehensive auditory processing and perceptual performance testing and questionnaires. A number of additional tests (hearing tests, intelligence tests, language tests) will be performed before/at baseline to differentiate from other disorders and to detect common comorbidities.

interventions.name: 24 children with dyslexia receive a RMHS (remote microphone hearing systems) for 12 weeks additionally to a conventional learning therapy, the latter administered by a certified dyslexia therapist (usually a logopedist, psychologist, or teacher) (case group)

24 children with dyslexia undergo a conventional learning therapy only (control group).
Group assignment of children with dyslexia between Group I and II is randomized.
15 children with auditory processing difficulties associated with hyperacusis/misophonia receive a RMHS for 12 weeks
15 children with auditory processing difficulties associated with an autism spectrum disorder receive a RMHS for 12 weeks
15 children with auditory processing difficulties associated with learning/intellectual/multiple disabilities which include learning or intellectual disabilities receive a RMHS for 12 weeks

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
(1) a peripheral hearing loss has been excluded by pure tone audiometry assessing air conduction and bone conduction thresholds at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 kHz (for 8 kHz air conduction only),
(2) and auditory processing capabilities have been assessed by a phoniatric-audiological and psychological standard testing using a test battery that involves:
a. speech audiometry in quiet and in noise (Oldenburger Satztest, OLSA or Oldenburger Kindersatztest, OLKISA in noise and Göttinger Kindersprachverständnistest or Freiburger Test für Einsilber in quiet)
b. the dichotic listening test by Uttenweiler or Feldmann, depending on age 
c. the Mottier Test
d. the subtest Repetition of Numbers (BASIC-MLT)
e. the Verbal learning and memory test (VLMT, Hogrefe Verlag)
f. the subtests Sentence Repetition, Rhyming, Substitution of Vowels, and Elision of Consonants from the Potsdam-Illinois Test für Psycholinguistische Fähigkeiten (P-ITPA; Ballaschk et al. 2010) [Potsdam-Illinois Test of Psycholinguistic Abilities]
g. the subtests Completion of Words (auditory completion), Connecting Sounds (auditory synthesis) from the Psycholinguistischer Entwicklungstest (PET) [Psycholinguistic development test]
h. the subtests on discrimination of speech stimuli (Place of Articulation, Voicing of Consonants - binaural) and on just noticeable differences of non-speech stimuli (Tone Duration, Frequency - interaural, Sinusoidal Amplitude Modulation - dichotic) from the Bochum Auditory and Speech Discrimination (BASD) Screening, and 
i. the subtest Auditory Discrimination from the neuropsychological screening test battery BVN/NPS
(3) a dyslexia (groups I and II) has been diagnosed by a logopedic and/or psychological standard testing using
a. the Hamburger Schreibprobe (HSP) [Hamburg Writing Sample] to record orthographic structure knowledge and spelling strategies
b. the reading test from Salzburger Lese- und Rechtschreibtest II (SLRT-II) [Salzburg Reading and Spelling Test II] for reading fluency of words ans pseudowords
c. the subtests Word Comprehension (decoding, synthesis), Sentence Comprehension (reading with understanding of the content, syntactic abilities), and Text Comprehension (identifying the information, sentence-overarching reading, deductive thinking) from the Ein Leseverständnistest für Erst- bis Sechstklässler (ELFE 1-6) [reading comprehension test for first- to  sixt-graders]
(4) a misophonia/hyperacusis (group III) as has been diagnosed by detailed measurements of loudness discomfort levels (LDLs) across the hearing range from 125 to 8 kHz and by the German self-rating questionnaire for the evaluation of hyperacusis, misophonia, and noise sensitivity (Mini-Hyperacusis Questionnaire (Mini-HQ9)
(5) an ASD (group IV) has been diagnosed before by a pediatric-psychological standard assessment 
(6) a learning or intellectual disability or multiple disabilities which include learning or intellectual disability (group V) has/have been diagnosed by 
• a nonverbal intelligence test using either the Wechsler Nonverbal Scales of Ability (WNV) or the Raven’s Progressive Matrices (RPM), and/or the CFT 1-R (Culture Fair Intelligence Test - Resivion) 
• a thorough pediatric assessment (eventually including other expertise such as psychological, radiological, genetic)
(7) parents or guardians and – if appropriate – children have given their written consent for participation in the study.
Exclusion criteria:
Unstable medical conditions or conditions that would place the individual or the examiner at risk for injury, lack of cooperation, or lack of consent of the subject or the parents, teachers or the legal guardian.
